content: If sodium delivery is a concern, such as when serum sodium levels exceed 145 mEq/L, consider using intravenous potassium phosphates to replenish phosphorus levels. Administering solutions containing both sodium and phosphorus in patients with impaired renal function may lead to hypernatremia or hyperphosphatemia. Lanthanum carbonate reduces the effects of intravenous sodium phosphates by binding cations in the gastrointestinal tract and is contraindicated. Lanthanum carbonate also lowers serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Similarly, sevelamer decreases the effects of intravenous sodium phosphates through cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract and is contraindicated. Sevelamer also reduces serum phosphate levels by binding dietary phosphate. Intravenous sodium phosphates can reduce the absorption of baloxavir marboxil due to cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Avoid or use an alternative drug, as baloxavir may bind to polyvalent cations, decreasing its absorption. Animal studies have shown that concurrent use with calcium, aluminum, or iron significantly reduces plasma levels, though human studies are lacking. Benazepril increases the toxicity of intravenous sodium phosphates through pharmacodynamic synergy. Avoid or use an alternative drug, as ACE inhibitors may enhance the nephrotoxic effects of sodium phosphate. Similarly, captopril and sodium phosphates, when used together, may increase each other's toxicity through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Avoid or use an alternative drug, as ACE inhibitors can exacerbate nephrotoxicity. Erdafitinib and intravenous sodium phosphates should not be co-administered during the initial dosing adjustment period (the first 21 days), as increases in serum phosphate levels are a pharmacodynamic effect of FGFR inhibition. Serum phosphate binders may obscure decisions regarding dosage adjustments. Calcium carbonate, calcium citrate, and calcium gluconate reduce the effects of intravenous sodium phosphates by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. These calcium compounds also lower serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Use alternatives if available. Dichlorphenamide and intravenous sodium phosphates both decrease serum potassium levels and may increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy. Both drugs can cause metabolic acidosis, so therapy should be modified and closely monitored. Furosemide reduces the effects of intravenous sodium phosphates by increasing renal clearance, thereby lowering serum phosphate levels. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is advised. Use alternatives if available. Magnesium citrate and magnesium hydroxide reduce the effects of intravenous sodium phosphates by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. These agents also lower serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Use alternatives if available. Intravenous sodium phosphates may decrease the effects of pseudoephedrine through an unknown mechanism. Caution is advised, and monitoring is recommended. Urinary excretion of indirect-acting alpha/beta agonists like pseudoephedrine may increase when administered with urinary acidifying agents, leading to lower serum concentrations. Voclosporin and intravenous sodium phosphates may increase each other's toxicity through nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Co-administration with nephrotoxic drugs may heighten the risk of acute or chronic nephrotoxicity. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is essential. High concentrations of phosphorus can cause hypocalcemia and hypocalcemic tetany; calcium levels should be monitored. Intravenous sodium phosphates must be diluted and thoroughly mixed before administration. Infuse solutions containing sodium phosphates slowly to avoid hypernatremia or hyperphosphatemia. Exercise caution in patients with severe renal or adrenal insufficiency, as they are at risk for sodium retention, hypernatremia, or hyperphosphatemia. Use with extreme care, if at all, in patients with conditions such as congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, or severe renal insufficiency, which are associated with sodium retention. Sodium phosphates should not be administered unless the solution is clear and the seal is intact. Discard any unused portion. Phosphorus plays a critical role in numerous biochemical functions, including metabolic and enzymatic reactions in nearly all organs and tissues. It influences calcium homeostasis, acid-base equilibrium, and renal hydrogen ion excretion. Sodium, the primary extracellular cation, is essential for regulating extracellular and intravascular volume. Calcium and phosphorus are incompatible and may precipitate in most aqueous solutions. Consult a pharmacist for guidance on mixing these components in total parenteral nutrition (TPN) admixtures. Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted with sodium phosphates, and it is unknown whether sodium phosphates can harm a fetus or affect reproductive capacity. Sodium phosphates should only be administered to pregnant women if clearly needed. Phosphorus and sodium are normal components of human milk. In cases of overdose, if serious symptoms such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing occur, call emergency services immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard expired or unused products. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs.
